The Mountain View City Council, by unanimous vote, placed this measure on the ballot.

If approved by a majority of voters, the measure would amend the Mountain View City Charter
to update and modernize several of its provisions. A city charter functions as the city's local
constitution by establishing the city's form of government and certain rules for its operation.

The proposed amendments would correct typographical errors, replace gender-specific terms
with gender-neutral language, improve consistency throughout the Charter, update outdated

terminology, and revise provisions to better reflect current state law and City practices. In
addition, the measure would make the following specific changes to the Mountain View Charter:

e clarify that the term "qualified elector" as used on the Charter has the same meaning as
the term “elector” under California law;

e extend the period for the City Council to fill a vacancy on the Council by appointment or
calling a special election from 30 days to 60 days;

e remove the requirement that ordinances and resolutions, or their titles, be read before
adoption;

* revise Charter Section 515 to require a roll-call vote on ordinances only when requested
by a Councilmember or otherwise required by law;

e update Section 709 to remove outdated references to maintaining “books” and instead
refer generally to City records;

e authorize the City Council to establish membership qualifications for boards,
commissions, and committees that are created by ordinance or resolution while retaining
existing membership requirements for the boards and commissions established by the
Charter;

e clarify the staggered-term requirements for boards, commissions, and committees in
Section 902;

e clarify that action by a board, commission, or committee shall be taken by majority vote
of the members then in office, excluding vacant positions, provided that the number of
members then in office is not less than a quorum of the entire membership; and

e revise one provision in the Community Stabilization and Fair Rent Act to update references
to the Mountain View City Code.

The above statement is an impartial analysis of Measure . If you desire a copy of the measure,
please call the City of Mountain View City Clerk’s Office at 650-903-6304, and a copy will be

mailed at no cost to you.

CITY ATTORNEY’S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS OF MEASURE F

Measure “ _” was placed on the ballot by a unanimous vote of the Mountain View City Council.
This measure asks the voters to approve an ordinance authorizing the City Council to increase
the Transient Occupancy Tax to a maximum rate of 15%. Measure “_” must be approved by a

majority of voters.

The City established a Transient Occupancy Tax in 1967. Chapter 33 of the Mountain View City
Code requires customers who stay in a hotel in the City for less than thirty (30) days to pay a
Transient Occupancy Tax, also known as hotel tax. The operators of these lodgings collect this
tax as part of the room bills and pay the tax to the city. A hotel includes any hotel, inn, tourist
home or house, motel or similar lodging. This hotel tax also applies to short-term rentals.

The voters last approved an increase to the hotel tax in 1991. The current Transient Occupancy
Tax rate is 10%. The majority of the cities in Santa Clara County have Transient Occupancy
Taxes with tax rates ranging between 12% and 15.5%

All revenue generated by this tax would be placed in the City’s general fund and could be used
for any general governmental purpose. Examples of projects performed for general governmental
purpose include, but are not limited to, repairing potholes, streets and sidewalks, improving
police, fire and 911 emergency response services, supporting affordable housing, adding new
parks and providing general government services.

Based on historical Transient Occupancy Tax revenues, the city estimates each 1% increase in
Transient Occupancy Tax could generate an additional $1,100,000.00 in funding revenue for
general governmental purposes each year.

A “yes” vote would amend the Mountain View City Code to authorize the City Council to
increase the Transient Occupancy Tax rate up to a maximum of 15%. A “no” vote would reject
the proposed ordinance, and the Transient Occupancy Tax rate would remain at 10%.

The above statement is an impartial analysis of Measure __. If you desire a copy of the
ordinance or measure, please call the City Clerk’s office at (650) 903-6304 and a copy will

be mailed at no cost to you.

End

City Attorney’s Impartial Analysis of Measure J
for the November 3, 2026 Election

*** Start Analysis ***

Measure J, the City of Palo Alto Community Safety/Services Measure, would authorize a 0.5%
(one-half of one percent) increase to the transactions and use tax (commonly known as a sales
tax) in the City of Palo Alto. The Palo Alto City Council placed this measure on the ballot by
unanimous vote. This measure requires approval by a simple majority of voters voting on the
measure and will remain in effect unless it is repealed by the voters. The City estimates that this
measure will generate revenues of approximately $15.6 million per year.

Measure J is a general tax, meaning that proceeds of the tax will be deposited in the City’s
general fund and can be used for any lawful governmental purpose. In June 2026, the City
Council passed a resolution adopting advisory spending guidelines that stated the Council’s
intention to use the proceeds to purchase seven-acres of the Cubberley Community Center
from the Palo Alto Unified School District. The advisory spending guidelines also state Council’s
intention to modernize the Cubberley Community Center. The plan includes renovation of some
existing buildings, new construction, and new outdoor park spaces.

If approved, the new sales tax rate would become effective in April 2027.

Measure J changes nothing else about the local sales tax. What items are taxable, the method
of collection, implementation, exemptions, and other provisions would remain unchanged.

If this measure does not pass, the local sales tax will not increase by the 0.5% proposed in this
measure, and the City of Palo Alto will not receive an estimated $15.6 million in revenue per
year from the tax.

A “yes” vote is a vote to approve a 0.5% increase to the transactions and use tax (commonly
known as a sales tax) within the City.

A “no” vote is a vote not to approve the increase to the transactions and use tax.

Christopher D. Jensen
City Attorney
City of Palo Alto

City Attorney’s Impartial Analysis of Measure J
for the November 3, 2026 Election

*** Start Analysis ***

Measure J, the City of Palo Alto Community Safety/Services Measure, would authorize a 0.5%
(one-half of one percent) increase to the transactions and use tax (commonly known as a sales
tax) in the City of Palo Alto. The Palo Alto City Council placed this measure on the ballot by
unanimous vote. This measure requires approval by a simple majority of voters voting on the
measure and will remain in effect unless it is repealed by the voters. The City estimates that this
measure will generate revenues of approximately $15.6 million per year.

Measure J is a general tax, meaning that proceeds of the tax will be deposited in the City’s
general fund and can be used for any lawful governmental purpose. In June 2026, the City
Council passed a resolution adopting advisory spending guidelines that stated the Council’s
intention to use the proceeds to purchase seven-acres of the Cubberley Community Center
from the Palo Alto Unified School District. The advisory spending guidelines also state Council’s
intention to modernize the Cubberley Community Center. The plan includes renovation of some
existing buildings, new construction, and new outdoor park spaces.

If approved, the new sales tax rate would become effective in April 2027.

Measure J changes nothing else about the local sales tax. What items are taxable, the method
of collection, implementation, exemptions, and other provisions would remain unchanged.

If this measure does not pass, the local sales tax will not increase by the 0.5% proposed in this
measure, and the City of Palo Alto will not receive an estimated $15.6 million in revenue per
year from the tax.

A “yes” vote is a vote to approve a 0.5% increase to the transactions and use tax (commonly
known as a sales tax) within the City.

A “no” vote is a vote not to approve the increase to the transactions and use tax.

Christopher D. Jensen
City Attorney
City of Palo Alto
